# Revisiting the Propinquity Theory of Tie Formation: The Conserved Interaction Budget and the Boundary-Selective Collapse of Cross-Functional Ties

## 1. Introduction

When a large, functionally differentiated organization moves its entire workforce from shared offices to full-time remote work, it runs an involuntary experiment on the communication network that holds it together. Knowledge-intensive firms integrate across functional units through a dense web of cross-boundary contacts, and the capacity to sustain those contacts is central to coordination, joint problem-solving, and innovation [(Whittington et al., 2009)](#ref-20). Understanding what a co-location shock does to the *internal structure* of that network — not merely to how much people communicate, but to whom — is therefore both theoretically and practically consequential.

The setting examined here is a single large technology company whose workforce shifted from co-located offices to full-time remote work. Employees' work-related contacts remained concentrated within their own functional group: the number of contacts linking employees across functional groups fell sharply, while contacts among employees within the same functional group stayed the same or increased. Strikingly, total logged working hours and total meeting time were almost unchanged between the two periods. The organization's interaction did not shrink — it reorganized. What changed was the composition of contact, not its volume, and the change was selective: it fell on ties that cross functional boundaries while sparing those contained within them.

The theory that speaks most directly to this setting is the physical proximity (propinquity) theory of interpersonal tie formation. Its central claim is that proximity raises tie formation and tie strength by increasing the number and frequency of spontaneous interaction opportunities [(Reagans, 2011)](#ref-13); [(Roche et al., 2024)](#ref-15); [(Catalini, 2018)](#ref-2). That volume-based mechanism predicts that removing co-location should depress interaction broadly. The observation that cross-functional contact collapsed while total logged hours and meeting time held constant therefore sits in direct tension with the theory's core premise — that proximity governs *how much* interaction occurs rather than *which ties* it flows through. We treat this premise as a challengeable assumption and ask why losing co-location selectively collapses cross-boundary ties while preserving within-unit ties and total volume, and whether proximity in fact governs the *composition* of organizational interaction rather than its volume. The paper develops a conserved-interaction-budget account in which role-mandated ties survive the shock and discretionary, ambient-prompted cross-boundary ties are triaged away.

## 2. Theory and Hypotheses

### Theoretical foundations

Propinquity theory holds that physical proximity encourages tie formation and strengthening because co-presence multiplies the spontaneous opportunities through which people encounter one another. Reagans [(2011)](#ref-13) shows that propinquity raises tie strength and amplifies the effect of social similarity, explicitly invoking increased communication frequency as the mechanism. Roche et al. [(2024)](#ref-15) find that the effect is short-range and decays quickly — start-ups more than roughly twenty meters apart on the same floor behave like those on different floors — and attribute it to social interaction among co-present peers. Catalini [(2018)](#ref-2) shows that colocation raises the likelihood of new joint research roughly 3.5-fold, an effect driven by pairs facing high ex-ante search costs, while Chai and Freeman [(2019)](#ref-3) show that temporary colocation primarily benefits pairs with no prior ties. Across this work, proximity operates by expanding the *opportunity* for interaction and thereby its amount.

The tradition has well-established boundary conditions. The proximity effect is documented mainly for the *formation* of new ties rather than the survival of established ones: separation does not reduce collaboration among previously colocated labs even as it makes their research trajectories less correlated [(Catalini, 2018)](#ref-2), and the benefits of temporary colocation accrue chiefly to pairs without prior ties [(Chai & Freeman, 2019)](#ref-3). The effect is short-range [(Roche et al., 2024)](#ref-15) and contingent on other forms of embeddedness, benefiting firms only when they are simultaneously embedded in physically distant networks [(Whittington et al., 2009)](#ref-20) and combining interactively with social similarity [(Reagans, 2011)](#ref-13). Finally, its absence can be partly offset by substitutes such as temporary colocation events and digital communication, whose effects on intra-group tie strength and extra-group reach depend on group dispersion and technology support [(Suh et al., 2011)](#ref-17).

Two internal tensions are especially relevant. The first is between *opportunity* and *choice*: the dominant explanation for network change is the supply of interaction opportunities, yet Kleinbaum [(2018)](#ref-10) names this premise explicitly and then shows that network change is also driven by actors' *tie-decay choices* conditional on opportunity. The second is whether losing co-location is benign or actively fragmenting — Catalini [(2018)](#ref-2) finds separation largely harmless for established collaboration, whereas Zuzul et al. [(2025)](#ref-22), analyzing over 360 billion emails across 4,361 organizations through the pandemic, find that remote work raised network modularity and that employees "limited their communication to other members of that community." The composition shift is thus now documented empirically, and Suh et al. [(2011)](#ref-17) already model intra-group strength and extra-group range as outcomes of virtuality. What the tradition lacks is an *account* of why the composition of contact would shift while its total volume is conserved: its mechanism routes proximity through the amount of interaction, and a volume mediator cannot generate a pattern in which totals hold constant while only the boundary-crossing subset collapses.

The theory developed here locates the explanation inside the anchor tradition itself, revisiting a part of it that has been assumed but never systematically developed. Kleinbaum's [(2018)](#ref-10) tie-decay account implies that, once the opportunity structure is reorganized, actors make deliberate choices about which ties to keep. We take that choice premise seriously and specify the currency in which the choice is made: actors hold a *finite capacity for tie maintenance*, and they allocate that capacity across ties according to how strongly each tie is embedded in their formal role. Ties whose upkeep is mandated by the workflow — principally, though not exclusively, within-unit workflow ties — elicit scheduled contact regardless of physical setting, because the work itself forces the interaction. Ties that are not mandated — principally, though not exclusively, cross-unit ties — were historically sustained at near-zero marginal cost by *ambient co-present cues*: seeing a colleague, passing them, an incidental check-in. When co-location is withdrawn, the ambient prompt disappears, and the now-unprompted tie must compete for bounded maintenance effort against role-mandated ties. Actors triage: discretionary cross-boundary ties lapse and the freed effort is reinvested within the unit. The assumptions are stated plainly: tie maintenance is effort-limited; effort is allocated preferentially to role-embedded ties; and the maintenance of cross-boundary ties depended on an ambient prompt rather than on the tie's recognized value.

Two constructs must be kept analytically distinct for this mechanism to be testable. A *boundary-crossing tie* is any work-related contact between members of different formal functional subunits; a *role-mandated tie* is a dyadic contact that the two members' documented workflows require — for example, a shared deliverable with a handed-off task. These correlate but need not coincide, and the theory's operative distinction is between mandated and discretionary maintenance, with the functional boundary as the place where mandate most reliably aligns with non-crossing. Crucially, mandate status can be classified *ex ante*, from process and workflow documentation and role-interdependency records, independently of whether a tie subsequently survived; a tie is not re-labeled as mandated merely because it persisted. This makes the mechanism operationalizable against its own most diagnostic cases — cross-unit but mandated ties — rather than protected by definition. The premises are consistent with adjacent work showing that physical space structures both the opportunities for and the strategies of social interaction [(Gonsalves, 2023)](#ref-6); that workspace design can build or strain relationships [(Khazanchi et al., 2018)](#ref-8); that some ties run on tacit coordination rather than on built communication channels [(Srikanth & Puranam, 2011)](#ref-16); that shared knowledge and presence awareness mitigate the coordination costs of distance [(Espinosa et al., 2007)](#ref-5); that cross-boundary understanding is cocreated around material work settings [(Bechky, 2003)](#ref-1) and carried by shared vocabularies [(Tasselli et al., 2020)](#ref-18); that boundary-spanning coordination is effortful and its absence invites costs [(Kellogg et al., 2006)](#ref-7); [(Marrone et al., 2007)](#ref-12); and that network structure emerges from opportunities *and* choices [(Zaheer & Soda, 2009)](#ref-21).

The account is a reallocation under a conserved total: total maintenance effort is bounded, and its distribution shifts toward within-unit ties rather than its level falling. This is what distinguishes it from the volume mechanism at the heart of propinquity theory and from media-substitution accounts, which concern the fit between channels and tasks rather than the composition of the network [(Dennis et al., 2008)](#ref-4); [(Van Osch & Steinfield, 2018)](#ref-19). Because the budget is conserved, the totality of logged hours and meeting time need not move; because the role boundary is the line between mandated and discretionary ties, the decay is boundary-selective.

### Research hypotheses

If the role of co-location is to supply the ambient, near-zero-cost prompts that keep discretionary cross-boundary ties alive, then withdrawing co-location should strip the boundary-crossing share of contact while leaving role-mandated within-unit ties untouched, since those are driven by the workflow rather than by the setting. This asymmetry is precisely what a volume-based proximity mechanism cannot predict, because it forecasts a broad decline [(Reagans, 2011)](#ref-13); [(Roche et al., 2024)](#ref-15), whereas a maintenance-choice account anticipates a compositional reshuffle [(Kleinbaum, 2018)](#ref-10).

**H1: The withdrawal of co-location reduces the share of work-related contact that crosses functional boundaries, even when total interaction volume is unchanged.**

The reallocation logic carries a second, separable implication. If maintenance effort is conserved and cross-boundary ties lose the competition for it, the freed effort must reappear as intensified within-unit interaction; the conserved-total claim is a prediction in its own right, not a restatement of the observed data, and it can be tested against a flat within-unit surface combined with an expanding total budget, which would refute conservation. This zero-sum signature is the account's most falsifiable element and the feature that separates it from explanations that posit a straightforward capability deficit [(Tasselli et al., 2020)](#ref-18); [(Espinosa et al., 2007)](#ref-5).

**H2: The reduction in cross-boundary contact is absorbed by an increase in within-unit contact, so that total contact volume is conserved.**

The magnitude of the reallocation should depend on how closely the functional boundary coincides with the boundary of formal role mandates. Where cross-unit ties are themselves mandated — matrix structures, cross-functional product teams, liaison roles — they should resist the shock, because their maintenance is compelled by the work rather than prompted by the setting, and the ambient-prompt account should lose its explanatory purchase [(Gonsalves, 2023)](#ref-6); [(Khazanchi et al., 2018)](#ref-8).

**H3: The reduction in cross-boundary contact is stronger where functional boundaries coincide with the boundaries of formal role mandates, and weaker where cross-boundary ties are themselves role-mandated.**

## 3. Theoretical Contribution

This study makes three contributions by reframing what physical proximity actually governs in organizational networks.

First, it contributes to propinquity theory by shifting the dependent variable from the *volume* of interaction to its *composition*. The tradition's dominant mechanism is a volume mediator — proximity raises frequency, and frequency sustains ties [(Reagans, 2011)](#ref-13); [(Roche et al., 2024)](#ref-15) — which cannot generate a pattern in which total logged hours and meeting time are conserved while only the boundary-crossing subset collapses. By locating the effect in the allocation of a bounded tie-maintenance budget across role-mandated and discretionary ties, the account shows that proximity can order *which* ties are maintained without changing *how much* interaction occurs, thereby addressing the theory's own unresolved tension between opportunity and choice [(Kleinbaum, 2018)](#ref-10).

Second, it contributes a mechanism to the organizational-network literature on composition. That virtuality reshapes intra-group strength and extra-group range [(Suh et al., 2011)](#ref-17), and that the pandemic raised modularity across thousands of organizations [(Zuzul et al., 2025)](#ref-22), are now established findings; what has been missing is a reason why the composition of the network shifts while its volume is preserved. The conserved-interaction-budget account fills this gap by specifying the currency of triage (mandated versus ambient-prompted maintenance) and the line along which it falls (the boundary of formal role mandates). It thereby connects the structural fact of fragmentation to a deliberate choicemaking process, extending the network-evolution tradition's own insight that structure emerges from opportunities and choices jointly [(Zaheer & Soda, 2009)](#ref-21); [(Kleinbaum, 2018)](#ref-10).

Third, it contributes to work on distributed and virtual organizing by decoupling volume from connectivity. If cross-boundary connectivity is carried by ambient prompts rather than by scheduled interaction, then preserving total interaction — holding meeting time constant or adding meetings — cannot restore it, and interventions must either supply substitutes for the lost prompt or embed cross-boundary ties in formal roles [(Gonsalves, 2023)](#ref-6); [(Srikanth & Puranam, 2011)](#ref-16); [(Van Osch & Steinfield, 2018)](#ref-19). This reframes the managerial problem of remote work from one of maintaining communication to one of maintaining boundary-crossing composition.

## 4. Boundary Conditions and Future Research

A first boundary condition concerns the alignment between the functional boundary and the boundary of formal role mandates. The theory is most precisely stated in terms of mandated versus discretionary maintenance, and it predicts that reallocation is strongest where the functional boundary coincides with the mandate boundary. In many large technology firms, however, cross-functional product work is itself role-mandated, so a portion of the collapsed cross-boundary ties may have been mandate-anchored rather than ambient-dependent. This is a design and measurement limitation rather than a conceptual one: the present evidence does not permit each dyad's mandate status to be classified independently of whether the tie survived. Future research could address this by obtaining ex ante workflow-interdependency and role-dependency records and testing whether the collapse concentrates among non-mandated cross-boundary dyads, and by studying settings in which the functional boundary and the mandate boundary are deliberately decoupled, such as matrix organizations, cross-functional product teams, and liaison roles.

A second boundary condition concerns the conservation premise. The claim that tie-maintenance effort is conserved, and that freed effort is absorbed within the unit, is inferred here from the observation that total logged hours and meeting time were unchanged. In settings where the maintenance budget can expand — salaried knowledge workers who work longer when remote, or organizations that increase meeting load — the conserved-budget premise degrades from a mechanism into an empirical coincidence, and the zero-sum prediction of H2 may fail while the compositional shift persists. Future research could test the zero-sum implication directly with within-person, longitudinal designs that track cross-boundary withdrawal and within-unit intensification simultaneously, and could use expandable-budget settings as a discriminating case between conservation and mere coincidence.

A third boundary condition concerns an alternative reading of the collapse: cross-boundary ties may have lapsed not because an ambient prompt was withdrawn but because their recognized value was genuinely lower. The theory assumes that maintenance of cross-boundary ties depended on a low-cost prompt rather than on the tie's value, and the present evidence cannot fully rule out the value-based alternative. A design that experimentally supplies prompts — scheduled cross-functional introductions, visibility tools, or engineered opportunities for co-presence [(Lane et al., 2021)](#ref-11); [(Kim et al., 2021)](#ref-9) — and observes whether lapsed ties recover would separate the prompt account from a value account. More broadly, the phenomenon is observed in a single organization across a single shock; its generalization to firms with different functional structures, and its persistence as remote work becomes permanent, remain open empirical questions [(Richter et al., 2006)](#ref-14).

### Full reasoning trail note

This run's Step 4⇄5 loop history contains a single recorded round at its conclusion. The interrogated candidate was the finally-selected one (Conserved Interaction Budget); the round's overall verdict was **weak** — the core directional claim was judged to hold, but several load-bearing premises were judged unresolved. The correspondence between that round's findings and the changes carried into the body is as follows.

- The two falsifiability exchanges and the boundary-conditions exchange objected that the identity "role boundary = mandated/discretionary boundary" was asserted rather than defended, and that no independent measurement rule existed to classify a tie's mandate status prior to observing its fate. This was addressed directly in Section 2 by (a) splitting *boundary-crossing* and *role-mandated* into analytically distinct constructs and making mandate-versus-discretion the operative distinction, (b) adding an ex ante classification rule (process/workflow documentation and role-interdependency records) that does not depend on tie survival, and (c) formalizing the contingency as the H3 moderation, which predicts exactly the cross-unit-but-mandated cases the interrogation flagged as most diagnostic. The residual, focal-setting validity concern (cross-functional work in large tech firms is often itself mandated) was moved to Section 4 as a design limitation.
- The second falsifiability exchange objected that "conserved total maintenance effort" was inferred from the observed unchanged totals and that its zero-sum implication was only half-supported. This was addressed in Section 2 by stating conservation as an independent prediction (H2) with an explicit falsification criterion — a flat within-unit surface combined with an expanding total budget would refute it. The residual, within-person evidence requirement was moved to Section 4.
- The relabeling-suspicion exchange showed that the composition outcome and the boundary-selective pattern are already empirically established (Zuzul et al., 2025; Suh et al., 2011) and that the original "why existing is insufficient" argument overreached. This was addressed in Section 3 by recalibrating the contribution from *outcome* novelty to *mechanism* novelty (why composition shifts while volume is conserved) and by citing those composition-based works explicitly in the theoretical foundations and contribution rather than omitting them.
- The unresolved alternative that cross-boundary ties lapsed because their recognized value was genuinely lower — which writing cannot rule out — was carried into Section 4 as a boundary condition with an experimental remedy (supplying prompts and observing recovery).

The complete question-by-question interrogation record is preserved in the system audit log.

## Phenomenon card
actor: A large technology company and its workforce — employees, organized into different functional groups, who communicate with one another in the course of their jobs.
observed_behavior: After the entire workforce moved from working in shared offices to working full-time from separate locations, employees' work-related contacts stayed mostly within their own functional group and changed little from one period to the next, instead of reaching across different functional groups.
field_constraints: The whole workforce of one large technology company; the change was a shift to full-time remote work; internal records of employees' communication were collected both before and after the shift; total logged working hours and total meeting time were almost the same in the two periods.
apparent_motive: (none — the phenomenon has no attributable actor)

## Research question (step 3)
Anchor theoretical direction: Propinquity / physical proximity theory of interpersonal tie formation
Research approach: problematization
Research question: Why does removing physical co-location from an entire organization's workforce — while total logged working hours and meeting time are preserved — selectively collapse ties that cross functional boundaries while leaving ties within functional units intact or strengthened? And does this imply that physical proximity governs the *composition* of organizational interaction (which boundaries are crossed) rather than its *volume*?

Rationale: The four directions were examined in the given order. Direction 1 (propinquity) returned exact-mechanism literature and was selected as the anchor; directions 2-4 returned substantial but miss-oriented literature and were judged not to carry the puzzle (recorded above).

**Why direction 1 does not simply "fully explain" the phenomenon.** Part of this literature does document the phenomenon at scale — Zuzul et al. (2025) find remote work raised communication-network modularity across 4,361 organizations, and Suh et al. (2011) show virtuality reshapes intra-group tie strength and extra-group network range. But the specific signature of this phenomenon is not covered: the effect is *boundary-selective*. Losing co-location collapsed cross-functional ties while within-function ties stayed flat or rose, with total logged hours and meeting time unchanged. A targeted search pairing proximity with cross-group/cross-functional/intergroup ties yields essentially no on-point work, so the boundary-selective outcome variable is genuinely unaddressed.

**Why problematization rather than gap-spotting.** Applying both lenses to the retrieved literature: the dominant stated mechanism is proximity -> interaction (Reagans, 2011; Roche et al., 2024), and network-evolution work names this the "interaction opportunities" logic (Kleinbaum, 2018). That makes the direction more than a void — the literature *does* explain the phenomenon, but on an assumption (proximity operates through the amount/opportunity of interaction) that the phenomenon's "unchanged totals" sits in direct tension with. Per the A&S guidance, when a problematization and a gap-spotting outcome both hold, problematization is preferred. Critically, this is not a forced or "prepackaged" problematization: the alternative assumption is constructed from the retrieved literature itself (Catalini, 2018, finds separation does *not* reduce collaboration between previously colocated labs, and that colocation instead drives new cross-cutting research trajectories; Chai and Freeman, 2019, find temporary colocation primarily enables collaborations between researchers with *no prior* ties), i.e., it points toward a composition/search reading rather than a volume reading. The alternative assumption passes Davis's three-way test (it partly affirms that proximity matters while denying the volume-mediator premise).

**Why not the safer mechanism_gap/anomalous_reversal framing.** A gap-spotting reading is defensible (one could argue the theory's opportunity logic predicts a general decline while the observation is a selective one — an anomalous reversal for the within-unit subset). I preferred problematization because the literature already documents the phenomenon, making "it covers it, but on a challengeable assumption" a more accurate characterization than "its mechanism doesn't cover this part." An honest caveat: the alternative assumption risks reading as obvious if collapsed into "proximity determines who you meet"; its genuinely non-obvious content is the *decoupling* of interaction volume from cross-boundary connectivity, which directly negates the frequency-based mechanism statements in Reagans (2011) and Roche et al. (2024).

## The anchor theory's deep-retrieval state (produced in step 3 — the deep retrieval done on the anchor theoretical direction itself, the main evidence for writing the 'what is the existing theoretical tradition, why is it insufficient' part of the 'Theoretical Foundations' section)
Anchor theory: Propinquity / physical proximity theory of interpersonal tie formation
Established boundary conditions: - The proximity effect is documented primarily for the *formation of new* ties/collaborations, not for the survival of established ones: Catalini (2018) finds colocation raises new joint research 3.5x but that separation does not reduce collaboration among previously colocated labs; Chai and Freeman (2019) find temporary colocation mainly benefits pairs with no prior ties.

- The effect is short-range and decays quickly: Roche et al. (2024) find start-ups more than ~20 meters apart on the same floor behave like those on different floors.

- Proximity's effect is contingent on other embeddedness: Whittington et al. (2009) show its innovation benefit depends on simultaneous embedding in a physically distant (global) network; Reagans (2011) shows it amplifies (interacts with) social similarity rather than acting alone.

- Ordinary distance/synchrony limits can be partly offset: temporary colocation events substitute for permanent proximity (Chai & Freeman, 2019; Kneeland & Kleinbaum, 2025), and digital 'virtuality' reshapes intra-group tie strength and extra-group range, moderated by group dispersion and technology support (Suh et al., 2011).
Internal tensions/gaps: 1. **Opportunity vs. choice.** The field's dominant explanation is 'interaction opportunities' (Kleinbaum, 2018, states this explicitly as what 'most research on network evolution' assumes), yet Kleinbaum (2018) shows network change is also driven by actors' *tie decay choices* conditional on opportunity — an internal challenge to the pure-opportunity premise.

2. **Benign vs. fragmenting separation.** Catalini (2018) finds separation does *not* harm collaboration among previously colocated labs (only making their research trajectories less correlated), whereas Zuzul et al. (2025) find the pandemic remote shift *fragmented* intraorganizational networks (increased modularity). Whether losing co-location is benign for existing structure or actively fragmenting is unresolved.

3. **Shared blind spot — composition, not volume of interaction.** No retrieved paper theorizes the *differential* effect of proximity loss on cross-boundary versus within-boundary ties. The targeted query pairing proximity with cross-group/cross-functional/intergroup tie types returns essentially no on-point organizational work, so the outcome variable in this literature is overall tie formation/collaboration, never the boundary-crossing *composition* of the network. This is precisely where the anchor theory's unresolved tension sits, and where Step 4's candidate theory is most worth cutting in.

### Candidate "Conserved Interaction Budget: Discretionary Ties Decay as Effort Reallocates to Role-Anchored Ties" (selected)

Ties whose maintenance is mandated by the formal role — principally within-unit workflow ties — elicit scheduled contact regardless of physical setting, because the work itself forces the interaction. Ties not mandated by the role — principally cross-unit ties — were sustained largely by ambient, near-zero-cost co-presence cues (seeing someone, passing them, incidental check-ins). When co-location is withdrawn the ambient prompt disappears, and the now-unprompted cross-unit tie must compete for the actor's bounded maintenance effort against role-mandated ties. # Revisiting the Propinquity Theory of Tie Formation: The Conserved Interaction Budget and the Boundary-Selective Collapse of Cross-Functional Ties

## 1. Introduction

Para 1 (background): The rise of full-time remote work has transformed how organizational members communicate. Modern firms are increasingly knowledge-intensive and functionally differentiated, and their capacity to integrate across functions depends on a dense web of cross-boundary communication ties. When workers share a physical workplace, incidental co-presence is woven into the fabric of daily work; when the entire workforce moves to separate locations, an important class of organizational interaction is put at risk. Understanding what happens to the internal communication network under such a shock matters for coordination, innovation, and organizational design [(Whittington et al., 2009)](#ref-20).

Para 2 (phenomenon): Setting: a large technology company. Observed: after the workforce moved from shared offices to full-time remote work, employees' work-related contacts remained concentrated within their own functional group; cross-functional contacts fell sharply, while within-functional contacts stayed the same or increased. Critically, total logged working hours and total meeting time were roughly unchanged between the two periods. So the organization's communication did not shrink; it reorganized — a compositional shift rather than a volume reduction.

Para 3 (research gap, names anchor theory): Propinquity theory — the theory of how physical proximity shapes tie formation — offers the most natural explanation and has established that proximity raises tie strength and collaboration by increasing interaction frequency/opportunities [(Reagans, 2011)](#ref-13); [(Roche et al., 2024)](#ref-15); [(Catalini, 2018)](#ref-2). The conserved totals contradict that assumption. This suggests proximity may govern the composition rather than the volume of interaction. Research question: why does removing co-location selectively collapse cross-boundary ties while preserving within-unit ties and total volume? We problematize the volume-mediator assumption and propose a conserved-interaction-budget account.

# Revisiting the Propinquity Theory of Tie Formation: The Conserved Interaction Budget and the Boundary-Selective Collapse of Cross-Functional Ties

## 1. Introduction

When a large, functionally differentiated organization moves its entire workforce from shared offices to full-time remote work, it runs an involuntary experiment on the communication network that holds it together. Knowledge-intensive firms integrate across functional units through a dense web of cross-boundary contacts, and the capacity to sustain those contacts is central to coordination, joint problem-solving, and innovation [(Whittington et al., 2009)](#ref-20). Understanding what a co-location shock does to the *internal structure* of that network — not merely to how much people communicate, but to whom — is therefore both theoretically and practically consequential.

The setting examined here is a single large technology company whose workforce shifted from co-located offices to full-time remote work. Employees' work-related contacts remained concentrated within their own functional group: the number of contacts linking employees across functional groups fell sharply, while contacts among employees within the same functional group stayed the same or increased. Strikingly, total logged working hours and total meeting time were almost unchanged between the two periods. The organization's interaction did not shrink — it reorganized. What changed was the composition of contact, not its volume, and the change was selective: it fell on ties that cross functional boundaries while sparing those contained within them.

The theory that speaks most directly to this setting is the physical proximity (propinquity) theory of interpersonal tie formation. Its central claim is that proximity raises tie formation and tie strength by increasing the number and frequency of spontaneous interaction opportunities [(Reagans, 2011)](#ref-13); [(Roche et al., 2024)](#ref-15); [(Catalini, 2018)](#ref-2). That volume-based mechanism predicts that removing co-location should depress interaction broadly. The observation that cross-functional contact collapsed while total logged hours and meeting time held constant therefore sits in direct tension with the theory's core premise — that proximity governs *how much* interaction occurs rather than *which ties* it flows through. We treat this premise as a challengeable assumption and ask why losing co-location selectively collapses cross-boundary ties while preserving within-unit ties and total volume, and whether proximity in fact governs the *composition* of organizational interaction rather than its volume. The paper develops a conserved-interaction-budget account in which role-mandated ties survive the shock and discretionary, ambient-prompted cross-boundary ties are triaged away.

## 2. Theory and Hypotheses

### Theoretical foundations

Propinquity theory holds that physical proximity encourages tie formation and strengthening because co-presence multiplies the spontaneous opportunities through which people encounter one another. Reagans [(2011)](#ref-13) shows that propinquity raises tie strength and amplifies the effect of social similarity, explicitly invoking increased communication frequency as the mechanism. Roche et al. [(2024)](#ref-15) find that the effect is short-range and decays quickly — start-ups more than roughly twenty meters apart on the same floor behave like those on different floors — and attribute it to social interaction among co-present peers. Catalini [(2018)](#ref-2) shows that colocation raises the likelihood of new joint research roughly 3.5-fold, an effect driven by pairs facing high ex-ante search costs, while Chai and Freeman [(2019)](#ref-3) show that temporary colocation primarily benefits pairs with no prior ties. Across this work, proximity operates by expanding the *opportunity* for interaction and thereby its amount.

The tradition has well-established boundary conditions. The proximity effect is documented mainly for the *formation* of new ties rather than the survival of established ones: separation does not reduce collaboration among previously colocated labs even as it makes their research trajectories less correlated [(Catalini, 2018)](#ref-2), and the benefits of temporary colocation accrue chiefly to pairs without prior ties [(Chai & Freeman, 2019)](#ref-3). The effect is short-range [(Roche et al., 2024)](#ref-15) and contingent on other forms of embeddedness, benefiting firms only when they are simultaneously embedded in physically distant networks [(Whittington et al., 2009)](#ref-20) and combining interactively with social similarity [(Reagans, 2011)](#ref-13). Finally, its absence can be partly offset by substitutes such as temporary colocation events and digital communication, whose effects on intra-group tie strength and extra-group reach depend on group dispersion and technology support [(Suh et al., 2011)](#ref-17).

Two internal tensions are especially relevant. The first is between *opportunity* and *choice*: the dominant explanation for network change is the supply of interaction opportunities, yet Kleinbaum [(2018)](#ref-10) names this premise explicitly and then shows that network change is also driven by actors' *tie-decay choices* conditional on opportunity. The second is whether losing co-location is benign or actively fragmenting — Catalini [(2018)](#ref-2) finds separation largely harmless for established collaboration, whereas Zuzul et al. [(2025)](#ref-22), analyzing over 360 billion emails across 4,361 organizations through the pandemic, find that remote work raised network modularity and that employees "limited their communication to other members of that community." The composition shift is thus now documented empirically, and Suh et al. [(2011)](#ref-17) already model intra-group strength and extra-group range as outcomes of virtuality. What the tradition lacks is an *account* of why the composition of contact would shift while its total volume is conserved: its mechanism routes proximity through the amount of interaction, and a volume mediator cannot generate a pattern in which totals hold constant while only the boundary-crossing subset collapses.

The theory developed here locates the explanation inside the anchor tradition itself, revisiting a part of it that has been assumed but never systematically developed. Kleinbaum's [(2018)](#ref-10) tie-decay account implies that, once the opportunity structure is reorganized, actors make deliberate choices about which ties to keep. We take that choice premise seriously and specify the currency in which the choice is made: actors hold a *finite capacity for tie maintenance*, and they allocate that capacity across ties according to how strongly each tie is embedded in their formal role. Ties whose upkeep is mandated by the workflow — principally, though not exclusively, within-unit workflow ties — elicit scheduled contact regardless of physical setting, because the work itself forces the interaction. Ties that are not mandated — principally, though not exclusively, cross-unit ties — were historically sustained at near-zero marginal cost by *ambient co-present cues*: seeing a colleague, passing them, an incidental check-in. When co-location is withdrawn, the ambient prompt disappears, and the now-unprompted tie must compete for bounded maintenance effort against role-mandated ties. Actors triage: discretionary cross-boundary ties lapse and the freed effort is reinvested within the unit. The assumptions are stated plainly: tie maintenance is effort-limited; effort is allocated preferentially to role-embedded ties; and the maintenance of cross-boundary ties depended on an ambient prompt rather than on the tie's recognized value.

Two constructs must be kept analytically distinct for this mechanism to be testable. A *boundary-crossing tie* is any work-related contact between members of different formal functional subunits; a *role-mandated tie* is a dyadic contact that the two members' documented workflows require — for example, a shared deliverable with a handed-off task. These correlate but need not coincide, and the theory's operative distinction is between mandated and discretionary maintenance, with the functional boundary as the place where mandate most reliably aligns with non-crossing. Crucially, mandate status can be classified *ex ante*, from process and workflow documentation and role-interdependency records, independently of whether a tie subsequently survived; a tie is not re-labeled as mandated merely because it persisted. This makes the mechanism operationalizable against its own most diagnostic cases — cross-unit but mandated ties — rather than protected by definition. The premises are consistent with adjacent work showing that physical space structures both the opportunities for and the strategies of social interaction [(Gonsalves, 2023)](#ref-6); that workspace design can build or strain relationships [(Khazanchi et al., 2018)](#ref-8); that some ties run on tacit coordination rather than on built communication channels [(Srikanth & Puranam, 2011)](#ref-16); that shared knowledge and presence awareness mitigate the coordination costs of distance [(Espinosa et al., 2007)](#ref-5); that cross-boundary understanding is cocreated around material work settings [(Bechky, 2003)](#ref-1) and carried by shared vocabularies [(Tasselli et al., 2020)](#ref-18); that boundary-spanning coordination is effortful and its absence invites costs [(Kellogg et al., 2006)](#ref-7); [(Marrone et al., 2007)](#ref-12); and that network structure emerges from opportunities *and* choices [(Zaheer & Soda, 2009)](#ref-21).

The account is a reallocation under a conserved total: total maintenance effort is bounded, and its distribution shifts toward within-unit ties rather than its level falling. This is what distinguishes it from the volume mechanism at the heart of propinquity theory and from media-substitution accounts, which concern the fit between channels and tasks rather than the composition of the network [(Dennis et al., 2008)](#ref-4); [(Van Osch & Steinfield, 2018)](#ref-19). Because the budget is conserved, the totality of logged hours and meeting time need not move; because the role boundary is the line between mandated and discretionary ties, the decay is boundary-selective.

### Research hypotheses

If the role of co-location is to supply the ambient, near-zero-cost prompts that keep discretionary cross-boundary ties alive, then withdrawing co-location should strip the boundary-crossing share of contact while leaving role-mandated within-unit ties untouched, since those are driven by the workflow rather than by the setting. This asymmetry is precisely what a volume-based proximity mechanism cannot predict, because it forecasts a broad decline [(Reagans, 2011)](#ref-13); [(Roche et al., 2024)](#ref-15), whereas a maintenance-choice account anticipates a compositional reshuffle [(Kleinbaum, 2018)](#ref-10).

**H1: The withdrawal of co-location reduces the share of work-related contact that crosses functional boundaries, even when total interaction volume is unchanged.**

The reallocation logic carries a second, separable implication. If maintenance effort is conserved and cross-boundary ties lose the competition for it, the freed effort must reappear as intensified within-unit interaction; the conserved-total claim is a prediction in its own right, not a restatement of the observed data, and it can be tested against a flat within-unit surface combined with an expanding total budget, which would refute conservation. This zero-sum signature is the account's most falsifiable element and the feature that separates it from explanations that posit a straightforward capability deficit [(Tasselli et al., 2020)](#ref-18); [(Espinosa et al., 2007)](#ref-5).

**H2: The reduction in cross-boundary contact is absorbed by an increase in within-unit contact, so that total contact volume is conserved.**

The magnitude of the reallocation should depend on how closely the functional boundary coincides with the boundary of formal role mandates. Where cross-unit ties are themselves mandated — matrix structures, cross-functional product teams, liaison roles — they should resist the shock, because their maintenance is compelled by the work rather than prompted by the setting, and the ambient-prompt account should lose its explanatory purchase [(Gonsalves, 2023)](#ref-6); [(Khazanchi et al., 2018)](#ref-8).

**H3: The reduction in cross-boundary contact is stronger where functional boundaries coincide with the boundaries of formal role mandates, and weaker where cross-boundary ties are themselves role-mandated.**

## 3. Theoretical Contribution

This study makes three contributions by reframing what physical proximity actually governs in organizational networks.

First, it contributes to propinquity theory by shifting the dependent variable from the *volume* of interaction to its *composition*. The tradition's dominant mechanism is a volume mediator — proximity raises frequency, and frequency sustains ties [(Reagans, 2011)](#ref-13); [(Roche et al., 2024)](#ref-15) — which cannot generate a pattern in which total logged hours and meeting time are conserved while only the boundary-crossing subset collapses. By locating the effect in the allocation of a bounded tie-maintenance budget across role-mandated and discretionary ties, the account shows that proximity can order *which* ties are maintained without changing *how much* interaction occurs, thereby addressing the theory's own unresolved tension between opportunity and choice [(Kleinbaum, 2018)](#ref-10).

Second, it contributes a mechanism to the organizational-network literature on composition. That virtuality reshapes intra-group strength and extra-group range [(Suh et al., 2011)](#ref-17), and that the pandemic raised modularity across thousands of organizations [(Zuzul et al., 2025)](#ref-22), are now established findings; what has been missing is a reason why the composition of the network shifts while its volume is preserved. The conserved-interaction-budget account fills this gap by specifying the currency of triage (mandated versus ambient-prompted maintenance) and the line along which it falls (the boundary of formal role mandates). It thereby connects the structural fact of fragmentation to a deliberate choicemaking process, extending the network-evolution tradition's own insight that structure emerges from opportunities and choices jointly [(Zaheer & Soda, 2009)](#ref-21); [(Kleinbaum, 2018)](#ref-10).

Third, it contributes to work on distributed and virtual organizing by decoupling volume from connectivity. If cross-boundary connectivity is carried by ambient prompts rather than by scheduled interaction, then preserving total interaction — holding meeting time constant or adding meetings — cannot restore it, and interventions must either supply substitutes for the lost prompt or embed cross-boundary ties in formal roles [(Gonsalves, 2023)](#ref-6); [(Srikanth & Puranam, 2011)](#ref-16); [(Van Osch & Steinfield, 2018)](#ref-19). This reframes the managerial problem of remote work from one of maintaining communication to one of maintaining boundary-crossing composition.

## 4. Boundary Conditions and Future Research

A first boundary condition concerns the alignment between the functional boundary and the boundary of formal role mandates. The theory is most precisely stated in terms of mandated versus discretionary maintenance, and it predicts that reallocation is strongest where the functional boundary coincides with the mandate boundary. In many large technology firms, however, cross-functional product work is itself role-mandated, so a portion of the collapsed cross-boundary ties may have been mandate-anchored rather than ambient-dependent. This is a design and measurement limitation rather than a conceptual one: the present evidence does not permit each dyad's mandate status to be classified independently of whether the tie survived. Future research could address this by obtaining ex ante workflow-interdependency and role-dependency records and testing whether the collapse concentrates among non-mandated cross-boundary dyads, and by studying settings in which the functional boundary and the mandate boundary are deliberately decoupled, such as matrix organizations, cross-functional product teams, and liaison roles.

A second boundary condition concerns the conservation premise. The claim that tie-maintenance effort is conserved, and that freed effort is absorbed within the unit, is inferred here from the observation that total logged hours and meeting time were unchanged. In settings where the maintenance budget can expand — salaried knowledge workers who work longer when remote, or organizations that increase meeting load — the conserved-budget premise degrades from a mechanism into an empirical coincidence, and the zero-sum prediction of H2 may fail while the compositional shift persists. Future research could test the zero-sum implication directly with within-person, longitudinal designs that track cross-boundary withdrawal and within-unit intensification simultaneously, and could use expandable-budget settings as a discriminating case between conservation and mere coincidence.

A third boundary condition concerns an alternative reading of the collapse: cross-boundary ties may have lapsed not because an ambient prompt was withdrawn but because their recognized value was genuinely lower. The theory assumes that maintenance of cross-boundary ties depended on a low-cost prompt rather than on the tie's value, and the present evidence cannot fully rule out the value-based alternative. A design that experimentally supplies prompts — scheduled cross-functional introductions, visibility tools, or engineered opportunities for co-presence [(Lane et al., 2021)](#ref-11); [(Kim et al., 2021)](#ref-9) — and observes whether lapsed ties recover would separate the prompt account from a value account. More broadly, the phenomenon is observed in a single organization across a single shock; its generalization to firms with different functional structures, and its persistence as remote work becomes permanent, remain open empirical questions [(Richter et al., 2006)](#ref-14).
